lesson.title: Undoing the Tangent: The Arctan Integral Pattern
lesson.summary: The integral of 1/(1+x²) is arctan(x) + C, the most frequently used of the three inverse trig integrals because rational functions with x squared in the denominator show up constantly.
lesson.body:
The arctan integral comes from the same reverse derivative logic as the arcsin integral, just applied to a different familiar derivative: d/dx[arctan(x)] = 1/(1+x²). Flipping that around gives the integral of 1/(1+x²) dx equals arctan(x) + C. This is arguably the most commonly used of the three inverse trig integrals, because the shape of a constant plus x squared in a denominator shows up far more often in practice than square roots do, especially once you start working with rational functions that have irreducible quadratic denominators.

The general version replaces the 1 with a positive constant a²: the integral of 1/(a²+x²) dx is (1/a) arctan(x/a) + C. Check it with the chain rule: the derivative of (1/a) arctan(x/a) is (1/a) times (1/a) divided by (1+(x/a)²), which simplifies to 1/(a²+x²) once you multiply the denominator out to (a²+x²)/a² and clear the fractions. The leading factor of 1/a is easy to forget, so it is worth building the habit of checking your answer by differentiating it back.

Evaluate the integral of 1/(1+x²) dx from x = 0 to x = 1. The antiderivative is arctan(x), so the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus gives arctan(1) minus arctan(0). Since tan(π/4) = 1, arctan(1) = π/4, and arctan(0) = 0. The definite integral equals π/4 minus 0, or π/4, about 0.7854.

Now try a case with a constant other than 1. Evaluate the integral of 1/(3+x²) dx from x = 0 to x = √3. Here a² = 3, so a = √3, and the antiderivative is (1/√3) arctan(x/√3). Plugging in the bounds gives (1/√3) times [arctan(√3/√3) minus arctan(0/√3)], which is (1/√3) times [arctan(1) minus arctan(0)], which is (1/√3) times (π/4 minus 0), or π/(4√3). Numerically, √3 is about 1.732, so π divided by (4 times 1.732) is about 3.1416 divided by 6.928, which is about 0.4534. Notice the leading 1/a factor is what keeps this answer from simply being another multiple of π/4, and it is easy to lose that factor if you rush.

Like the arcsin integral, this pattern is the indefinite integral idea, antiderivative plus C, wrapped around one specific building block derivative. Whenever a rational function has a denominator that is a sum of squares, an irreducible quadratic that cannot be factored over the reals, arctan is the function that eventually undoes it.
